llm-foundations-q1.testing: the mechanism precisely, why three separate projections, and whether you can connect it to the compute and memory bill.
llm-foundations-q1.trap: "the model focuses on the important words" — that's the metaphor, not the mechanism.
llm-foundations-q1.spoken:
"Self-attention is a soft, learned dictionary lookup. For every token, the model computes three vectors by multiplying its embedding with three learned matrices: a query, which is what this position is looking for; a key, which is what it advertises to others; and a value, which is what it hands over if it's matched.

Each token's query is dotted with every key, the scores are divided by the square root of the key dimension so the softmax doesn't saturate, a causal mask blocks future positions in a decoder, and the softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to one. The output for that token is the weighted average of all the value vectors.

Why three matrices instead of one? Because 'what I'm looking for', 'what I match on' and 'what I pass along' are different jobs. Separate projections let a token match on, say, syntax, while passing along meaning. Multiple heads do this in several subspaces in parallel.

The win over recurrence is that every position reaches every other in one step, fully parallel in training. The cost is quadratic in sequence length for the score matrix, and at inference the keys and values of every past token must be kept in the KV cache. That's why long context is expensive, and why most serving optimisations — GQA, FlashAttention, paged KV caches — are about attention."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Each token's output is a weighted average of every visible token's value vector, with weights from query–key dot products."

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( QKᵀ / √d_k + mask ) · V
Q = X·W_Q    K = X·W_K    V = X·W_V        (same X: that's the "self")

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Piece Role Why it's separate
Query what this position is looking for asks the question
Key what each position offers for matching decides the weights
Value the content passed on when matched decides what's mixed in
√d_k keeps dot-product variance ~1 else softmax saturates, gradients vanish
causal mask −∞ on future positions decoders can't read ahead
multi-head h smaller attentions in parallel different relations in different subspaces
  • After the heads are concatenated, an output projection mixes them, and the result is added to the residual stream.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d_model, d_k = 4, 8, 4                       # 4 tokens (illustrative sizes)
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d_model))
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(d_model, d_k)) for _ in range(3))
Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)
scores[np.triu_indices(n, 1)] = -np.inf         # causal mask
A = np.exp(scores - scores.max(1, keepdims=True)); A /= A.sum(1, keepdims=True)
print(A.round(2)); print(A.sum(1), (A @ V).shape)
# → [[1.   0.   0.   0.  ]
#    [0.97 0.03 0.   0.  ]
#    [0.92 0.   0.08 0.  ]
#    [0.01 0.25 0.08 0.66]]
# → [1. 1. 1. 1.] (4, 4)

Row i is token i's weights: the upper triangle is zero (the mask), every row sums to 1. With random weights they're arbitrary; training shapes them.

stages.name: What it costs
stages.claim: n² compute, n memory per layer
stages.html:
Phase Cost Bottleneck
training / prefill O(n²·d) for the score matrix compute (and memory traffic, which FlashAttention fixes)
decode, per new token O(n·d) reading all cached K, V memory bandwidth
KV cache 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × n × bytes per sequence memory capacity
  • Double the context: prefill attention compute ×4, KV cache ×2.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
• Long prompts raise time-to-first-token (prefill) and cut concurrency (KV cache). Trim context deliberately, don't fill the window by default.
  • Model choice: GQA/MQA models have smaller KV caches, so more concurrent users per GPU.
  • The same mechanism underlies failure modes you'll debug: attention dilution in long contexts, and "lost in the middle".

followUps.question: 🧪 A 32-layer model, 8 KV heads of dimension 128, fp16. How big is the KV cache for one 8k-token conversation?
followUps.html: 2 (K and V) × 32 × 8 × 128 × 8,192 × 2 bytes = 1,073,741,824 bytes ≈ 1 GiB per sequence (illustrative config, close to Llama-3-8B-class models). Ten such conversations need ~10 GiB just for cache.

followUps.question: "Attention tells us which words the model thinks are important."
followUps.html: Attention weights show how values were mixed in one head of one layer, not an explanation of the output. Many heads do positional or syntactic bookkeeping, and the residual stream and MLPs carry much of the computation. Use them as a debugging hint, not as an explanation.

followUps.question: Why divide by √d_k?
followUps.html: With unit-variance entries, a dot product of two d_k-dimensional vectors has variance d_k. Large scores push the softmax into near one-hot, where gradients vanish. Dividing by √d_k brings the variance back to about 1. See Q41.

followUps.question: Why several heads instead of one big head?
followUps.html: One head produces one set of weights per token: one "question". Several heads with smaller dimensions ask several questions at once (a previous-token head, a coreference head) for about the same compute. See Q42.

followUps.question: What's the difference between self-attention and cross-attention?
followUps.html: In self-attention, Q, K and V all come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, Q comes from one sequence (the decoder) and K, V from another (the encoder's output or image features). It's how encoder–decoder models and many multimodal models connect two streams.

followUps.question: Your product sends 30k-token prompts and latency is bad. Which part of attention is hurting?
followUps.html: Prefill: 30k tokens of quadratic attention before the first output token, so time-to-first-token suffers. Then each decode step reads a large KV cache, so throughput per GPU drops. Levers: trim or cache the prompt prefix (provider prompt caching), retrieve less, choose a GQA model, and measure TTFT separately from tokens per second.

dontSay: "Attention focuses on important words" as the mechanism.
"Q, K and V are the same vector."

spine: What I'd pick for this system
llm-foundations-q2.testing: that you explain the win through the training objective, task generality and inference mechanics — and know it's per-role, not absolute.
llm-foundations-q2.trap: "decoder-only is simply the better architecture" — your embedding model and reranker are encoders.
llm-foundations-q2.spoken:
"The three families differ in two choices: the attention mask and the pretraining objective. Encoder-only models like BERT see the whole text in both directions and learn by filling in masked tokens. Encoder-decoders like T5 read the input bidirectionally and generate the output with a separate decoder. Decoder-only models use a causal mask and just predict the next token.

Decoder-only won generation for three reasons. First, training signal: next-token prediction gives a loss at every position of every sequence, on raw text, with no task design. BERT-style masking only supervises about 15 percent of tokens. Second, universality: every task — classification, extraction, translation, dialogue — becomes 'continue this text', so one model and one interface serve everything, and in-context learning falls out of that framing. Third, inference: with a causal mask the past never changes, so the key-value cache is simply appended to, which makes streaming generation cheap to serve.

But it's a win per role, not overall. For embeddings and reranking, bidirectional context is exactly right, so encoders are still the workhorses of retrieval. Encoder-decoders still make sense when input and output are genuinely different sequences.

So in a RAG system I'd typically run all of them in their place: an encoder for embeddings, a cross-encoder reranker, and a decoder-only model to generate."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: mask plus objective defines the family
stages.html:
Family Mask Objective Exemplar Natural job
encoder-only bidirectional masked-token prediction BERT embeddings, classification, reranking
encoder-decoder bidirectional encoder, causal decoder + cross-attention span corruption / seq2seq T5, many translation models input → different output sequence
decoder-only causal next-token prediction GPT family, Llama generation, in-context learning

stages.name: Where decoder-only wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — supervised positions per 1,024-token training sequence:

decoder-only (next token):     1,023 targets    (every position predicts the next)
BERT-style MLM (15% masked):     ~154 targets    (0.15 × 1,024)
→ ~6.6× more loss signal per sequence from the same text
  • Universality: one text-in/text-out interface; prompts and few-shot examples replace task heads.
  • Inference: the causal mask makes each new token's K, V an append; the cache never needs recomputing when a token is added.
  • Scaling simplicity: one stack, one objective, fewer design choices to get wrong at scale.

stages.name: Where encoders still win
stages.html:
• Embeddings: a bidirectional model sees the whole passage when forming each token's representation; retrieval quality depends on that.
  • Cross-encoder reranking: query and document read jointly, both directions, one relevance score.
  • Classification at scale: small encoders are cheap, fast and accurate for fixed label sets.
  • Decoder-based embedding models exist and do well on benchmarks, but they're adapted with bidirectional or pooling changes — the representation job still wants full context.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
• Output is free text or the task set is open → decoder-only.
  • Output is a vector, a score or a fixed label, and cost per call matters → encoder.
  • Input and output are distinct sequences with tight alignment (translation, speech) → encoder-decoder remains reasonable.

stages.name: What I'd pick for this system
stages.html: • The architect's point: "which architecture won" is the wrong question for a system; each stage picks the family that fits its output type.

followUps.question: 🧪 BERT masks 15% of tokens. For a 512-token sequence, how many positions give loss, versus a decoder?
followUps.html: About 77 for BERT (0.15 × 512) versus 511 for a decoder. Per token of text read, the decoder gets roughly 6–7× more training signal. That efficiency is a big part of why the objective scaled.

followUps.question: "So encoders are obsolete."
followUps.html: No — nearly every production retrieval stack runs an encoder for embeddings and often a cross-encoder reranker. They're smaller, faster and better suited to producing a representation than a generator is.

followUps.question: Why does the causal mask make KV caching easy?
followUps.html: A token's K and V depend only on itself and earlier tokens. Adding a new token doesn't change any earlier representation, so cached K, V stay valid and you only compute the new row. With bidirectional attention, a new token would change every earlier representation.

followUps.question: Where does in-context learning come from in this story?
followUps.html: From the continuation framing plus scale: web text contains many "examples then answer" patterns, so a next-token predictor learns to continue them. Encoders trained on masked tokens don't get a generation interface to exploit this.

followUps.question: Would you ever pick an encoder-decoder today?
followUps.html: For narrow seq2seq jobs at high volume — translation, summarisation to a fixed style, speech-to-text (Whisper is encoder-decoder) — a small encoder-decoder can be cheaper and more controllable than a general decoder. For open-ended assistants, a decoder-only model is the default.

dontSay: "Encoder-decoder is outdated" without the translation/speech caveat.

llm-foundations-q3.testing: the size formula, which factors grow, and the mitigations in the right order.
llm-foundations-q3.trap: "it caches the prompt" — it's per-layer K and V tensors, and it's your real memory budget.
llm-foundations-q3.spoken:
"During generation, each new token has to attend to all the previous tokens, which needs their key and value vectors in every layer. Without a cache, every decode step would recompute those for the whole prefix: quadratic work per token. The KV cache stores the keys and values of every past token, per layer and per KV head, so each new step only computes one new row and reads the rest.

Its size is two, for K and V, times layers, times KV heads, times head dimension, times sequence length, times bytes per value, times the number of concurrent sequences. The important part is what grows: it's linear in context length and linear in batch. For a typical 8-billion-parameter model it's around 128 kilobytes per token, so an 8k conversation is about a gigabyte, and 30 of those need more memory than the weights themselves.

That's why it dominates. Weights are a fixed cost; the KV cache is the variable cost of every user and every token of context. It decides how many concurrent requests fit on a GPU, and since every decode step re-reads it, it also makes decoding memory-bandwidth-bound.

Mitigations, in order: grouped-query attention reduces KV heads and is built into the model; paged attention removes fragmentation; KV-cache quantisation halves the bytes; and shorter prompts or prefix sharing reduce the tokens."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: the per-user, per-token memory of attention
stages.html: "The KV cache holds K and V for every past token in every layer; it trades O(n²) recompute for O(n) memory per sequence."

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: prefill fills it, decode appends and reads
stages.html:
• Prefill: the prompt's tokens are processed in parallel; their K, V for all layers are written to the cache.
  • Decode: each step computes Q, K, V for the new token only, appends K, V, and attends over the whole cache.
  • Only K and V are cached: past queries are never needed again.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: the size formula on a real-shaped model
stages.html:
bytes per token = 2 (K,V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes
Llama-3-8B-like: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 (fp16)       = 131,072 B ≈ 128 KiB / token
  × 8,192 tokens                                    ≈ 1 GiB per conversation
  × 32 concurrent conversations                     ≈ 32 GiB   (weights: ~16 GB in fp16)
Same model without GQA (32 KV heads instead of 8)   ≈ 4× → 512 KiB / token

stages.name: What it costs
stages.html:
Effect Why
fewer concurrent sequences GPU memory − weights = room for caches
decode is memory-bound every step reads the whole cache for every sequence
fragmentation naive allocation reserves max length per sequence
long context hurts twice bigger cache and more reads per token

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Lever Where it lives Saving
GQA / MQA model architecture (choose the model) KV heads ÷ 4–8
PagedAttention (vLLM) serving engine removes over-reservation and fragmentation
KV-cache quantisation (fp8/int8) serving engine ~2×
prefix caching serving engine / provider shared system prompts stored once
sliding-window attention model architecture caps tokens per layer
shorter prompts, smarter retrieval application fewer tokens
  • Serving details live in LLM-SERVING-INFERENCE.

followUps.question: 🧪 A GPU has 80 GB. Weights take 16 GB. At 128 KiB per token, how many concurrent 4k-token sequences fit, ignoring overhead?
followUps.html: 64 GB free ÷ (4,096 × 128 KiB = 512 MiB) ≈ 128 sequences. Double the context to 8k and it halves to about 64. That's the lever product decisions like "max context per user" pull on.

followUps.question: "The KV cache stores the prompt so we don't resend it."
followUps.html: It stores per-layer attention tensors for a sequence during generation. It doesn't persist across API requests by default; provider "prompt caching" is a separate feature that reuses computed prefixes across requests.

followUps.question: Why not cache Q too?
followUps.html: A token's query is used only once, when that token attends to the past. Later tokens need earlier tokens' keys and values, never their queries.

followUps.question: How does GQA reduce the cache without killing quality?
followUps.html: Several query heads share one K/V head, so there are fewer K, V tensors to store. Query heads keep their diversity. Studies and deployed models (Llama 2 70B onward) show quality close to full multi-head attention at a fraction of the KV size.

followUps.question: Your chat product wants to raise max context from 8k to 128k. What do you tell the PM?
followUps.html: Per-user KV memory grows 16×, so concurrency per GPU drops ~16× for users who use it, TTFT rises with prefill, and cost per conversation rises. Offer it as a tier or for specific features, cap it per plan, and check that quality at 128k is actually good for the task.

dontSay: "Memory is dominated by the weights" (at long context and high concurrency, it isn't).

llm-foundations-q4.testing: why attention needs position at all, the absolute-to-relative shift, and RoPE's link to context extension.
llm-foundations-q4.trap: not connecting RoPE to why long-context extension works at all.
llm-foundations-q4.spoken:
"Attention itself has no notion of order. It's a weighted sum over a set, so without position information 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look the same. Position has to be injected.

The original transformer added fixed sinusoidal vectors to the embeddings; later models learned absolute position embeddings. Both encode the absolute index, and learned ones don't work past the training length.

What language mostly needs is relative offset: this word is two before that one. RoPE, rotary position embedding, gets that elegantly. It rotates each pair of dimensions in the query and key by an angle proportional to the token's position, with different frequencies per pair. When you take the dot product of a rotated query at position m and a rotated key at position n, the rotations combine into a rotation by m minus n. So the attention score depends only on the relative distance, with no extra parameters.

That property is also why context extension works. Because position is an angle, you can rescale the angles — position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN — so longer sequences map into the range the model saw in training, then fine-tune briefly. That's how many models went from 4k or 8k to 128k. ALiBi is the other relative approach: it adds a distance penalty to attention scores instead."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: rotate Q and K so scores depend on offset
stages.html: "RoPE encodes position as a rotation of Q and K; their dot product then depends only on the distance between tokens."

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Scheme Where applied Absolute / relative Past training length
sinusoidal added to embeddings absolute degrades
learned absolute added to embeddings absolute no positions exist
ALiBi bias on attention scores, ∝ distance relative degrades gracefully
RoPE rotation of Q, K per dimension pair relative (via rotation) extendable by scaling
  • RoPE: pair dimensions (2i, 2i+1), rotate by angle pos × base^(−2i/d); low pairs spin fast (local order), high pairs spin slowly (long-range).

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: the same offset gives the same score, anywhere
stages.html:
import numpy as np
def rope(x, pos, base=10000):
    d = x.shape[-1]; theta = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d) * pos
    x1, x2 = x[0::2], x[1::2]; c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
    out = np.empty_like(x); out[0::2] = x1*c - x2*s; out[1::2] = x1*s + x2*c
    return out
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); q, k = rng.normal(size=8), rng.normal(size=8)
for m, n in [(5, 2), (105, 102), (1005, 1002), (5, 4)]:
    print(m, n, round(float(rope(q, m) @ rope(k, n)), 4))
# → 5 2 -1.5865
# → 105 102 -1.5865
# → 1005 1002 -1.5865
# → 5 4 -1.6954

Offset 3 gives the same score at positions 5, 105 and 1005; changing the offset changes the score.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
• Past the training length, the fast-spinning pairs are fine (they've seen every angle), but slow pairs reach angles never seen in training, and quality collapses.
  • Extension methods fix that: position interpolation (squeeze positions into the trained range), NTK-aware scaling (change the base so high-frequency pairs are preserved), YaRN (per-frequency interpolation plus attention temperature). All need a short fine-tune at longer length to be good.
  • An extended window isn't automatically a usable one: check retrieval accuracy at depth (see Q22, Q23).

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: ask how the window was extended and tested
stages.html:
• When choosing a long-context model, ask how it was extended and evaluated at length, not just the advertised number.
  • For self-hosting, RoPE scaling settings (e.g. rope_scaling in the model config) must match what the model was trained with; wrong settings degrade silently.

followUps.question: 🧪 Remove positional information entirely from a decoder. Does it still know order?
followUps.html: Somewhat. The causal mask itself leaks position: token i sees exactly i tokens, so models trained without explicit positions ("NoPE") learn some order. But explicit encodings work better and more reliably; every major LLM uses one. In an encoder without a mask, removing position makes it a bag of words.

followUps.question: "RoPE lets a model handle any length."
followUps.html: Only within what it was trained or fine-tuned on, plus modest extension. Beyond that, attention to unseen angles degrades. Extension needs scaling methods and fine-tuning, and effective recall still drops with length.

followUps.question: Why rotate Q and K but not V?
followUps.html: Position should affect who attends to whom (the scores), not the content being mixed. Rotating V would scramble the information passed along without helping the matching.

followUps.question: RoPE vs ALiBi?
followUps.html: ALiBi adds a linear distance penalty to scores: simple and extrapolates gracefully, but biases toward recency. RoPE keeps full expressiveness and has become the default in open decoder LLMs; its extension story (NTK, YaRN) is well developed.

followUps.question: A vendor offers a 1M-token version of a model you use. How do you evaluate it before adopting?
followUps.html: Run your own tasks at several depths and lengths: needle-style retrieval plus multi-fact reasoning over your real documents, compared with RAG over the same corpus. Measure quality, latency and cost per query. Adopt only where long context beats retrieval on your metrics.

dontSay: "RoPE adds a position vector to the embedding."
"Any RoPE model extrapolates to unlimited length."

llm-foundations-q5.testing: concrete production consequences — cost, context, numbers, languages, exact matching — not a BPE lecture.
llm-foundations-q5.trap: treating tokens as words when estimating cost or context.
llm-foundations-q5.spoken:
"Models don't see characters or words; they see tokens from a fixed vocabulary, usually built with byte-pair encoding. Frequent strings become single tokens, rare ones get split into several pieces.

It bites in four places. Cost and context: everything is billed and budgeted in tokens, and the ratio of tokens to words varies a lot. Non-English text can cost two or three times more than English, depending on the tokenizer — with an older OpenAI tokenizer a short Hindi sentence took 20 tokens versus 6 for its English equivalent; a newer one takes 9. So cost estimates don't transfer between models or languages.

Numbers: 12345678 becomes pieces like '123', '456', '78', so digits aren't aligned, which is part of why models make arithmetic errors that look like reasoning failures. Use a tool or code for maths.

Exact matching: product codes, IDs and rare names fragment in ways that hurt embedding similarity, which is one reason keyword search still earns a place next to dense retrieval.

And edge behaviour: leading spaces are part of tokens, so prompt formatting, stop sequences and constrained output interact with token boundaries in surprising ways.

In practice I always count tokens with the target model's tokenizer, per language, before sizing budgets."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "Tokenization maps text to IDs from a fixed vocabulary of subword pieces; the model's cost, context and some errors are all measured in those pieces."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
• BPE starts from bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair until the vocabulary size (e.g. 100k–200k) is reached.
  • The training corpus decides what's cheap: languages and domains well represented get long tokens.
  • Byte-level fallback means nothing is out-of-vocabulary, but rare text becomes many tokens.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the same text, two tokenizers (tiktoken):

import tiktoken
for name in ("cl100k_base", "o200k_base"):
    enc = tiktoken.get_encoding(name)
    print(name, [len(enc.encode(s)) for s in ["Hello, how are you?", "नमस्ते, आप कैसे हैं?", "12345678 + 87654321"]])
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
print([enc.decode([i]) for i in enc.encode("12345678 + 87654321")])
# → cl100k_base [6, 20, 8]
# → o200k_base [6, 9, 8]
# → ['123', '456', '78', ' +', ' ', '876', '543', '21']
Where Symptom Mitigation
cost / context budgets off by 2–3× for some languages count with the real tokenizer, per language
numbers digit chunks misaligned; arithmetic slips tools or code for maths; format numbers consistently
IDs, codes, rare names poor embedding similarity, misspelled outputs hybrid search (BM25), constrained decoding for IDs
whitespace and boundaries stop sequences or prefixes behave oddly test prompts at the token level; avoid trailing spaces
model switch different counts, different limits re-estimate cost when changing providers

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.claim: budgets per language, hybrid search for IDs
stages.html:
• Budgeting: token counts per request type and per language feed rate limits and cost forecasts.
  • Retrieval: hybrid search for SKU/ID-heavy queries where dense retrieval fragmented the codes.
  • Guardrails: truncating by tokens, not characters, so context limits aren't exceeded.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Logit bias, stop sequences and constrained decoding all operate on tokens; knowing boundaries is what makes them reliable (see Q11, Q12).

followUps.question: 🧪 Why might a model fail to count the letter 'r' in "strawberry"?
followUps.html: It doesn't see letters. In cl100k_base, "strawberry" is str | aw | berry, and " strawberry" with a leading space is a single token (checked with tiktoken). Letter counts inside tokens are only indirectly learned. Spelling tasks go through token-to-character knowledge the model may not have. Tools or character-level prompting help.

followUps.question: "A token is about a word."
followUps.html: Roughly 0.75 English words per token for common tokenizers, but code, numbers and many languages differ widely. Measure; don't use a rule of thumb for budgets.

followUps.question: Why not use characters or bytes directly?
followUps.html: Sequences would be 3–5× longer, and attention cost grows quadratically with length. Subwords compress text so more meaning fits per position. Byte-level models exist but pay that length cost.

followUps.question: Your support bot serves English and Hindi users at the same price. What's the problem?
followUps.html: Hindi users may cost 1.5–3× more per message depending on the model's tokenizer, and fill context faster. Measure per-language token ratios, price or rate-limit in tokens, and prefer models whose tokenizers cover your languages efficiently.

followUps.question: Can you add tokens to a model's vocabulary?
followUps.html: Yes, by extending the embedding and output matrices and fine-tuning so the new rows learn useful values. It helps for heavy domain terms or new scripts, but needs enough training data; otherwise the new tokens are worse than the split pieces.

dontSay: Cost estimates without naming the tokenizer.

llm-foundations-q6.testing: that you know it's exact attention with fewer memory reads and writes — a systems win, not a modelling one.
llm-foundations-q6.trap: calling it approximate or sparse attention.
llm-foundations-q6.spoken:
"FlashAttention computes exactly the same attention output; it just moves far less data. Standard attention writes the full n-by-n score matrix to GPU high-bandwidth memory, reads it back for the softmax, writes the probabilities, and reads them again to multiply by V. At long sequence lengths that traffic, not the arithmetic, is the bottleneck: GPUs can do math much faster than they can move data to and from HBM.

FlashAttention tiles the computation. It loads blocks of Q, K and V into the small, fast on-chip SRAM, computes scores for that block, and uses an online softmax — keeping a running maximum and a running sum — so it can combine blocks without ever materialising the full matrix. The output is identical up to floating-point rounding.

Two results: it's several times faster in practice, and the extra memory for attention goes from quadratic to linear in sequence length, because the n-squared matrix never exists. In training, the backward pass recomputes blocks instead of storing them, trading cheap compute for expensive memory.

What it doesn't change: the arithmetic is still quadratic, and the KV cache during decoding is untouched — that's a different problem. It's the reason long-context training and prefill became affordable, and it's on by default in modern serving engines, so as an application engineer I mostly benefit from it rather than configure it."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "FlashAttention computes exact attention while never writing the n×n score matrix to HBM; it fixes memory traffic, not the maths."

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Standard FlashAttention
S = QKᵀ written to HBM (n × n) score tiles live in SRAM only
softmax reads S, writes P (n × n) online softmax: running max and sum per row
O = PV reads P again O accumulated tile by tile
backward stores P backward recomputes tiles (Dao et al., 2022)
  • FlashAttention-2 improved work partitioning across GPU threads; FlashAttention-3 targets Hopper features (async, FP8).

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: the tiled online softmax gives the exact answer
stages.html:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); s = rng.normal(size=1024); v = rng.normal(size=1024)
full = (np.exp(s - s.max()) / np.exp(s - s.max()).sum()) @ v
m, l, acc = -np.inf, 0.0, 0.0                     # running max, normaliser, weighted sum
for blk in range(0, 1024, 128):                   # 8 tiles, never the full row at once
    sb, vb = s[blk:blk+128], v[blk:blk+128]
    m_new = max(m, sb.max()); scale = np.exp(m - m_new)
    p = np.exp(sb - m_new)
    l, acc, m = l * scale + p.sum(), acc * scale + p @ vb, m_new
print(round(float(full), 10), round(float(acc / l), 10), np.isclose(full, acc / l))
# → -0.0444781612 -0.0444781612 True

One query row, one value dimension: rescaling earlier partial sums when the max changes is the whole trick.

The memory it avoids (fp16, per head, per layer):

n = 32,768:  n² × 2 bytes = 2 GiB for one score matrix
× 32 heads = 64 GiB per layer if materialised at once

stages.name: What it doesn't change
stages.html:
• FLOPs are still O(n²·d); very long sequences are still compute-heavy.
  • Decode-time KV-cache size and bandwidth (Q3) are unaffected; PagedAttention and GQA address those.
  • Not sparse, not approximate: same model quality.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: you benefit from it more than you configure it
stages.html:
• Use serving engines and training stacks that ship it (vLLM, TGI, PyTorch SDPA backends); check GPU generation support.
  • It made long-context prefill affordable, but TTFT still grows with prompt length; don't treat it as free context.

followUps.question: 🧪 If FlashAttention does the same FLOPs, how can it be several times faster?
followUps.html: Because standard attention at long lengths is memory-bound: most time goes to reading and writing n² intermediates in HBM. Cutting HBM traffic lets the arithmetic units stay busy. Runtime tracks bytes moved, not FLOPs, when you're bandwidth-bound.

followUps.question: "FlashAttention is an approximate attention method."
followUps.html: It's exact up to floating-point rounding. Approximate methods (sparse, low-rank, linear attention) change the model's computation; FlashAttention changes only the execution plan.

followUps.question: Why does the backward pass recompute instead of storing?
followUps.html: Storing the n×n probabilities for backprop would reintroduce quadratic memory. Recomputing tiles from Q, K, V and the saved softmax statistics costs extra FLOPs but saves far more memory traffic, so it's faster overall.

followUps.question: Does it help decoding latency?
followUps.html: Much less. Decode computes one query row against the cache; the bottleneck is reading the KV cache. Variants like Flash-Decoding split the cache across thread blocks to parallelise that read, but the big wins are in prefill and training.

followUps.question: Does this change how you choose a model or a provider?
followUps.html: Indirectly. It's standard now, so it isn't a differentiator; what differs is how providers handle long-prompt prefill (TTFT at 50k tokens) and prompt caching. Benchmark TTFT at your real prompt sizes rather than trusting "supports long context".

llm-foundations-q7.testing: total vs active parameters, and that MoE saves compute, not memory.
llm-foundations-q7.trap: "MoE models are smaller" — they need more VRAM, not less.
llm-foundations-q7.spoken:
"In a mixture-of-experts transformer, the feed-forward block in each layer is replaced by several parallel feed-forward networks, the experts, plus a small router. For each token, the router scores the experts and sends the token to the top one or two. Attention is still dense; what's sparse is which expert weights each token uses.

So there are two parameter counts. Total parameters are large, which gives the model capacity. Active parameters per token are small, which sets the compute per token. Mixtral 8x7B is the classic example: about 47 billion total, about 13 billion active per token, so it runs with roughly the per-token compute of a 13B model.

What's not sparse is memory. All experts must be loaded, because the next token may need any of them. So you pay memory like a 47B model and compute like a 13B one.

There are real costs. Training needs load balancing — auxiliary losses — or the router collapses onto a few experts. Serving is harder: tokens in a batch go to different experts, so you need expert parallelism across GPUs, and utilisation is uneven. MoE pays off at high throughput on enough hardware; for a single small-GPU deployment, a dense model of similar active size is often simpler."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: sparse in compute, dense in memory
stages.html: "Each token uses only k of N expert FFNs, so compute follows active parameters while memory follows total parameters."

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
• Only the FFN is expert-ised in most designs; attention layers are shared.
  • Variants: fine-grained experts plus shared experts (DeepSeek-MoE style), top-1 routing (Switch Transformer).

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
tokens, d, n_exp, k = 6, 16, 8, 2
x = rng.normal(size=(tokens, d)); W_router = rng.normal(size=(d, n_exp))
top = np.argsort(-(x @ W_router), axis=1)[:, :k]
print(top.tolist())
print(np.bincount(top.ravel(), minlength=n_exp).tolist())
# → [[5, 1], [2, 3], [4, 1], [6, 1], [7, 4], [2, 6]]
# → [0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1]

Each token picks two experts; the load count shows expert 1 got 3 tokens and expert 0 none — the imbalance training must fight.

Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral AI, 2023):  ~46.7B total · ~12.9B active per token
Memory to hold weights (bf16):    46.7B × 2 B ≈ 93 GB   ← all experts resident
Compute per token:                ~ like a 13B dense model

stages.name: What it costs
stages.html:
Area Cost
memory every expert loaded; VRAM ~ total params
training load-balancing losses, router instability, capacity limits (dropped tokens)
serving expert parallelism, all-to-all communication, uneven expert load, harder batching
fine-tuning more fragile; LoRA on experts and router needs care

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: compare active params, memory and measured quality
stages.html:
• Via an API, MoE is invisible except in price and speed: often more quality per dollar.
  • Self-hosting: budget GPU memory for total params; throughput benefits appear with large batches across several GPUs.
  • Don't compare an MoE and a dense model by parameter count alone; compare active params, memory and measured quality.

followUps.question: 🧪 An MoE has 64 experts, top-2 routing, and each expert FFN is 100M params per layer. What fraction of FFN weights does one token touch per layer?
followUps.html: 2/64 ≈ 3% of the expert weights (200M of 6.4B) per layer, plus the shared attention weights. Compute per token scales with that 3%, but all 6.4B per layer must sit in memory.

followUps.question: "MoE models are cheaper to host because they're sparse."
followUps.html: Cheaper per token in compute, not in memory. A 47B-total MoE needs memory like a 47B model. Whether it's cheaper to host depends on reaching high enough utilisation to exploit the compute savings.

followUps.question: What is router collapse?
followUps.html: The router learns to send most tokens to a few experts, which then get more training and become even more attractive. Other experts stay untrained. Auxiliary load-balancing losses, noise in routing, and capacity limits counter it.

followUps.question: Do experts specialise in topics, like "a maths expert"?
followUps.html: Mostly not in a human-readable way. Analyses (e.g. in the Mixtral paper) find routing tracks syntax and token types more than domains. "Expert" is a name for a sub-network, not a subject specialist.

followUps.question: Would you self-host an MoE for an internal assistant with 200 users?
followUps.html: Probably not first. At low concurrency you pay full memory without the throughput benefit, and serving complexity is higher. A dense model of similar quality, or an API, is simpler. Revisit at higher traffic or if an MoE model is clearly better on your eval set.

dontSay: "Attention is split across experts" (in standard designs, it isn't).

llm-foundations-q8.testing: compute-optimal training, why models then went past it, and a sober view of "emergence".
llm-foundations-q8.trap: quoting emergent abilities as settled fact.
llm-foundations-q8.spoken:
"Scaling laws say that a language model's loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, training tokens and compute. That makes it predictable: you can fit curves on small runs and forecast what a bigger run will achieve.

Before Chinchilla, the influential Kaplan 2020 results suggested putting most extra compute into parameters. DeepMind's Chinchilla paper in 2022 redid the analysis and found that for a fixed compute budget, parameters and data should grow together — roughly 20 training tokens per parameter. By that measure, models like Gopher at 280 billion parameters were badly undertrained. Chinchilla, at 70 billion parameters trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, beat Gopher with the same compute.

Then the industry went further. Chinchilla optimises training compute, but a deployed model is run billions of times, so inference cost matters more. It's better to train a smaller model far past the compute-optimal point: Llama 3 8B was trained on about 15 trillion tokens, nearly 2,000 tokens per parameter. Smaller, longer-trained models are cheaper to serve.

On emergence: some abilities looked like they appeared suddenly with scale, but a 2023 paper showed that many jumps come from all-or-nothing metrics; with smoother metrics the curves are gradual. So I treat emergence as contested."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: loss is a power law in scale
stages.html: "Loss falls predictably as a power law in parameters N, tokens D and compute C ≈ 6·N·D; the laws tell you how to split a compute budget."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the arithmetic:

Training compute  C ≈ 6 × N × D            (forward + backward FLOPs)
Chinchilla rule   D ≈ 20 × N
Chinchilla 70B:   D ≈ 1.4T tokens → C ≈ 6 × 70e9 × 1.4e12 ≈ 5.9e23 FLOPs
Gopher 280B:      trained on ~300B tokens ≈ 1 token/param → undertrained
Llama 3 8B:       ~15T tokens (Meta, 2024) ≈ 1,875 tokens/param → deliberately "overtrained"

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
• They predict loss, not specific task ability; downstream skills track loss loosely.
  • Data quality and mixture shift the curves; "20 tokens/param" assumed a particular data distribution.
  • Data is running short: high-quality text is finite, hence synthetic data and multi-epoch training debates.
  • Emergence: Schaeffer et al. (2023) argue many "emergent" jumps are metric artefacts (exact-match scoring); with continuous metrics, improvement is smooth.

stages.name: How it shapes decisions
stages.html:
Goal Choice
best model for a fixed training budget Chinchilla-optimal N and D
cheapest model to serve at a quality bar smaller N, much larger D
application team choosing a model the small, heavily trained model often wins on cost per quality

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Reasoning models add a second axis: spending more compute at inference (longer thinking) also improves accuracy on some tasks (see Q19).

followUps.question: 🧪 You have 1e23 FLOPs. Using C ≈ 6ND and D = 20N, roughly what model size is compute-optimal?
followUps.html: C = 6 × N × 20N = 120N² → N = √(1e23 / 120) ≈ 2.9e10, so about 29B parameters on ~580B tokens. (A rough application of the rule; real fits vary.)

followUps.question: "Emergent abilities prove models suddenly gain new skills at scale."
followUps.html: Contested. Several apparent jumps disappear with continuous metrics. Some capabilities do improve sharply around certain scales, but "sudden emergence" is not settled fact.

followUps.question: Why is training past compute-optimal rational?
followUps.html: Because lifetime cost is training plus inference. If a model will serve trillions of tokens, a smaller model that took extra training compute to reach the same quality saves far more at inference.

followUps.question: What happens when we run out of high-quality text?
followUps.html: Options being used: multiple epochs over good data (diminishing returns after a few), synthetic data from stronger models, better filtering and deduplication, and more multimodal data. Each has limits; this is an open problem.

followUps.question: How do scaling laws affect your model choice as an application team?
followUps.html: They explain why smaller, recent models often match older larger ones: they're trained on far more data. So I benchmark small models first on my eval set and pay for larger ones only where the gap matters, because inference cost is what I pay every day.

dontSay: "Chinchilla says 20 tokens per parameter is optimal for deployment."

llm-foundations-q9.testing: the mechanics (temperature rescales logits, top-p cuts adaptively) and a task-based policy.
llm-foundations-q9.trap: raising temperature to "make it smarter" — it makes outputs less likely, not more correct.
llm-foundations-q9.spoken:
"At each step the model produces logits over the vocabulary, and decoding decides which token to pick. The knobs trade determinism for diversity.

Temperature divides the logits before the softmax. Below one it sharpens the distribution toward the top token; above one it flattens it; zero means greedy, always the most likely token. Top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens. Top-p, nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p — so it adapts: when the model is confident it keeps one or two tokens, when it's unsure it keeps many.

My policy is by task. Anything that feeds code — extraction, classification, tool arguments, JSON — gets temperature zero or close to it, ideally with constrained decoding, because I want the most likely answer every time. Summaries and Q&A get low temperature, around 0.2 to 0.5. Creative writing, brainstorming, or generating several candidates to pick from gets higher temperature, 0.7 to 1, with top-p around 0.9 to cut the absurd tail.

Two cautions: higher temperature doesn't make the model smarter, it just samples less likely tokens; and temperature zero isn't fully deterministic on GPUs. Also, many reasoning models fix or restrict these settings, so check the provider's guidance."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html: "Temperature reshapes the distribution; top-k and top-p truncate it. Together they set how often the model takes a less likely token."

stages.name: What each knob does
stages.claim: temperature reshapes, top-k and top-p truncate
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — five logits, several temperatures, and top-p:

import numpy as np
logits = np.array([4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.0])
def probs(t): z = np.exp((logits - logits.max()) / t); return z / z.sum()
for t in (0.2, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5):
    print(t, probs(t).round(3))
p = probs(1.0); order = np.argsort(-p); keep = order[: np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(p[order]), 0.9) + 1]
print("top-p 0.9 keeps tokens", keep.tolist())
# → 0.2 [0.993 0.007 0.    0.    0.   ]
# → 0.7 [0.761 0.182 0.044 0.01  0.003]
# → 1.0 [0.636 0.234 0.086 0.032 0.012]
# → 1.5 [0.505 0.259 0.133 0.068 0.035]
# → top-p 0.9 keeps tokens [0, 1, 2]
Knob Mechanism Adapts to confidence?
temperature T logits / T before softmax no, rescales everything
top-k keep k highest no, fixed count
top-p keep smallest set with mass ≥ p yes
min-p keep tokens ≥ p × top probability yes (newer, used in open-source stacks)

stages.name: Where low settings win
stages.html:
• Structured outputs, classification, extraction, tool calls, SQL: correctness is "the most likely answer"; sampling only adds errors.
  • Evaluation runs: lower variance makes comparisons meaningful.

stages.name: Where high settings win
stages.html:
• Creative text, varied phrasings, brainstorming.
  • Generating N diverse candidates to rank or vote on (self-consistency needs diversity).
  • Avoiding repetitive loops that greedy decoding can fall into on long open-ended text.

stages.name: What I'd set per task
stages.html:
Task Temperature Top-p
JSON / tool args / classification 0 (+ constrained decoding) 1
RAG answer, summary 0.1–0.4 1 or 0.9
chat assistant 0.5–0.8 0.9–0.95
creative / candidates for voting 0.8–1.0 0.9
  • Change one knob at a time, and version decoding settings with the prompt.

followUps.question: 🧪 With the logits above at T = 1, what's the chance of sampling token 4 with and without top-p 0.9?
followUps.html: Without truncation, 1.2%. With top-p 0.9 it's zero: only tokens 0–2 are kept (cumulative 0.956), and their probabilities are renormalised. That's how top-p cuts the long tail of odd tokens.

followUps.question: "Raise the temperature so the model is more creative and smarter."
followUps.html: Temperature changes which tokens get sampled, not what the model knows. Higher values add variety and also errors. For quality, improve the prompt, context or model.

followUps.question: Should you set both temperature and top-p?
followUps.html: You can, but tune one at a time. Some providers recommend altering only one. A common pairing is moderate temperature plus top-p 0.9–0.95.

followUps.question: What's the difference between greedy and beam search, and why don't chat models use beam?
followUps.html: Beam search keeps several high-probability partial sequences; it suits translation, where one correct output exists. For open-ended text it tends to produce bland, repetitive output, and it's expensive to serve, so chat uses sampling or greedy.

followUps.question: Your extraction pipeline gives different JSON for the same document on reruns. What do you change?
followUps.html: Temperature 0, constrained decoding to the schema, a pinned model version, and validation with a bounded repair. Accept that GPU non-determinism remains (Q10), so tests compare fields with tolerance, not raw strings.

dontSay: "Top-p and top-k are the same thing."

llm-foundations-q10.testing: that greedy decoding isn't bit-reproducible on shared GPU infrastructure, and that you design for tolerance.
llm-foundations-q10.spoken:
"Temperature zero means greedy decoding — take the highest-probability token — but greedy is only deterministic if the logits are bit-identical every time, and on GPUs they often aren't.

Floating-point addition isn't associative: adding the same numbers in a different order gives slightly different results. GPU kernels choose reduction orders based on batch size, sequence length and tiling. On a shared inference server, your request is batched with different other requests each time, so the numerics shift by tiny amounts. Usually that doesn't matter, but when two tokens are nearly tied, a tiny difference flips the argmax, and from that token on the whole continuation diverges.

There are other sources too: mixture-of-experts routing can depend on batch composition, speculative decoding and different hardware in the provider's fleet change numerics, and the provider may update the model behind the same name.

Before blaming the GPU, I rule out the fakes: is temperature really zero in the request, is top-p or a seed being set, is the prompt identical including timestamps or retrieved context, and is the model version pinned?

Then I design for it: pin model snapshots, use seeds where offered, constrain outputs to schemas, and write tests that compare meaning or fields with tolerance, never exact strings."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html: "Greedy picks the argmax; if two logits are nearly tied, reduction-order noise decides which one wins, and the rest of the output follows."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: check the request before blaming the GPU
stages.html:
Check Why it looks like the same symptom
request actually sends temperature: 0 SDK defaults, framework overrides
prompt byte-identical timestamps, IDs, retrieved chunks in different order
model version pinned alias like latest moved to a new snapshot
tools / retrieval deterministic a different search result changes the context

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the same sum in two orders, and a flipped argmax:

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=4096).astype(np.float32) * 100
a = np.float32(0)
for v in x: a += v                                 # reduction order 1 (sequential)
b = x.reshape(64, 64).sum(axis=1).sum()            # reduction order 2 (tiled, like another batch shape)
print(a, b, a == b)
rival = np.float32(-6606.465)                      # a competing token's logit, nearly tied
print(np.argmax([a, rival]), np.argmax([b, rival]))
# → -6606.468 -6606.461 False
# → 1 0
  • In production: run the same request 20 times; log logprobs of the top-2 tokens at the first divergence. A tiny gap there confirms it.

stages.name: Fix by design
stages.html:
Lever Effect
pinned model snapshot removes silent model changes
seed parameter (where offered) best-effort reproducibility, not a guarantee
constrained decoding + schema variation limited to valid values
cache responses by input hash identical requests return identical outputs
self-hosted: batch-invariant kernels, fixed batch size true determinism is possible at a throughput cost

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
• Compare parsed fields, not strings; semantic similarity or rubric-based checks for free text.
  • Run eval sets several times and report variance; gate on the mean with a confidence interval.

followUps.question: 🧪 Two runs at temperature 0 agree on the first 50 tokens, then diverge completely. Why complete divergence, not one word?
followUps.html: Autoregression: once one token differs, every later token is conditioned on a different prefix, so the continuations drift apart. The first divergent token is where the near-tie was.

followUps.question: "Set temperature to 0 and the eval is reproducible."
followUps.html: Not on shared GPU serving. Expect small run-to-run differences; measure variance and design tests with tolerance.

followUps.question: Why would batching change my result when my request is independent?
followUps.html: The kernels processing the batch choose different tiling and reduction orders for different batch shapes. Your sequence's arithmetic is then done in a different order, even though its inputs are the same.

followUps.question: Can you get full determinism?
followUps.html: Self-hosted, yes, with deterministic or batch-invariant kernels, fixed hardware, fixed batch sizes and no speculative decoding — at a throughput cost. With third-party APIs you get at best a seed-based "mostly".

followUps.question: Compliance wants the same answer for the same question. What do you offer?
followUps.html: Cache approved answers keyed by normalised input and model version, and serve from cache; pin the model; log input, output and version for audit. Don't promise that regeneration will be identical.

dontSay: "It must be a bug in our code" before checking numerics.

llm-foundations-q11.testing: that you constrain at decode time rather than parse and hope, and that "parses" isn't "correct".
llm-foundations-q11.spoken:
"The reliable way is to constrain decoding, not to parse afterwards. At every step, the model produces logits over the whole vocabulary. A constrained decoder compiles the JSON Schema into a grammar or state machine, works out which tokens are legal given what's been generated so far, and sets every other token's logit to minus infinity before sampling. The model literally cannot emit a token that breaks the schema: if it wants to start with 'Sure, here's the JSON', that token is masked and it has to start with a brace.

Providers expose this as structured outputs or strict tool schemas; self-hosted, vLLM's guided decoding, Outlines, XGrammar or llama.cpp grammars do the same.

Weaker options in order: JSON mode guarantees valid JSON but not your schema; prompting with examples plus parse-and-retry works most of the time but not always.

What constraining doesn't give you is correctness. The fields will parse, but the values can still be wrong — a hallucinated ID, a date in the wrong year. So I still validate with Pydantic, check business rules, and do a bounded repair with the validation errors before failing loudly.

Two costs to know: very complex schemas can be slow to compile or unsupported, and forcing a format the model finds unnatural can lower quality slightly — letting it reason in a field before the answer helps."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: mask illegal tokens at every step
stages.html: "Constrained decoding turns the schema into a token-level automaton and masks every token that would leave it; output is valid by construction."

stages.name: How constrained decoding works
stages.claim: the schema becomes a token-level automaton
stages.html:
Level Guarantees
prompt "reply in JSON" nothing
JSON mode syntactically valid JSON
schema-constrained (structured outputs, strict tools) valid against your schema's shape
+ Pydantic / business validation the constraints you encoded

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import numpy as np
vocab = ['{', '"', 'name', ':', 'Sure', '!', 'Here', '}']
logits = np.array([1.0, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0, 3.5, 2.0, 3.0, 0.1])   # model "wants" to say "Sure"
allowed = {'{'}                                                # grammar: JSON must start with {
mask = np.array([0 if t in allowed else -np.inf for t in vocab])
print(vocab[int(np.argmax(logits))], vocab[int(np.argmax(logits + mask))])
# → Sure {

stages.name: What it costs or misses
stages.html:
• Semantics: valid shape, possibly wrong values. Validate.
  • Quality: a rigid format can push the model off its natural phrasing; add a reasoning field first, or keep schemas simple.
  • Schema support: providers support subsets of JSON Schema (limits on recursion, oneOf, pattern keywords); check before designing.
  • Latency: compile time for new schemas; a small per-token overhead self-hosted.
  • Truncation: hitting max_tokens mid-object still yields incomplete output; check the finish reason.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: structured outputs plus validation plus bounded repair
stages.html:
• Default for anything code consumes: structured outputs + Pydantic validation + bounded repair (max 1–2) + typed failure.
  • Track schema-validation failure rate per model and prompt version (see guarantee-llm-output-shape for the service side).

followUps.question: 🧪 Your schema has . With constrained decoding, can the model output "Closed"?
followUps.html: No: after "status": ", only tokens continuing open or closed are legal. Without constraints, "Closed" is a common failure that fails validation.

followUps.question: "JSON mode is enough."
followUps.html: JSON mode guarantees parseable JSON, not your keys, types or enums. You need schema-constrained decoding plus validation.

followUps.question: Why might forcing JSON reduce answer quality?
followUps.html: The model can't "think" before answering if the first token must be { and the answer field comes first. Putting a free-text reasoning field before the answer field, or doing a two-step call, recovers most of the quality.

followUps.question: How does this work with tokens that span several characters?
followUps.html: The decoder precomputes, for each automaton state, which vocabulary tokens are consistent (a token like ":" covers several characters). Libraries like XGrammar and Outlines build these token-level masks efficiently so the per-step overhead is small.

followUps.question: Structured output fails 2% of the time in production. How do you handle it?
followUps.html: Find the cause first: truncation (raise max_tokens), unsupported schema features (simplify), or semantic validation failures (improve the prompt or add examples). Then a single repair call with the validation errors, a fallback model if the primary keeps failing, and a metric per prompt version so regressions show up after deploys.

dontSay: "I regex the JSON out of the response."

llm-foundations-q12.testing: concrete uses (classification scores, abstention, routing, highlighting) and the calibration caveat.
llm-foundations-q12.trap: treating a logprob as the probability that the answer is correct.
llm-foundations-q12.spoken:
"A logprob is the log of the probability the model assigned to the token it produced, and many APIs also return the top alternatives at each position. It's a cheap signal because it comes with the output.

Uses I've found practical. Classification: instead of asking for a label and parsing text, compare the logprobs of each label token, which gives a score per class and a margin. Abstention and routing: if the answer's key tokens have low probability or the top two are close, route to a bigger model, add retrieval, or ask a human. Highlighting: mark low-confidence spans in extracted fields for review. And evaluation: perplexity on held-out text, or scoring candidate answers.

The caveats matter. Logprobs measure the model's confidence in a token, not whether the claim is true; instruction-tuned models are often overconfident and confidently wrong. For whole answers you must normalise by length, because the joint probability of a long answer is always tiny even if every token is confident. And not every provider exposes them, especially for reasoning models, so I don't design systems that can't work without them.

So I use them as a feature: calibrate thresholds on a labelled set, and treat them as one signal among several."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "Logprobs are log P(token | prefix) for the chosen token and top alternatives; summed, they give the sequence's log-likelihood."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — why length normalisation is needed:

import math
short = [-0.1, -0.2]                               # token logprobs, 2-token answer
long = [-0.1] * 30 + [-0.2] * 10                   # 40-token answer, each token confident
for name, lp in [("short", short), ("long", long)]:
    total = sum(lp)
    print(name, round(math.exp(total), 3), round(math.exp(total / len(lp)), 3))
# → short 0.741 0.861
# → long 0.007 0.882

Joint probability says the long answer is "unlikely"; per-token geometric mean says it's as confident as the short one.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
Issue Why
overconfidence preference tuning sharpens distributions; high probability ≠ correct
paraphrase splits mass "Paris" vs "The capital is Paris": probability spread across phrasings
first-token only a label's first token may be shared by several labels
availability some APIs and reasoning models don't expose them, or only top-k
model changes thresholds need recalibration after upgrades

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.html:
• Label scoring: constrain output to label tokens and read their logprobs → a ranked score with no parsing.
  • Escalation: below a calibrated threshold, send to a stronger model or human review.
  • Field-level confidence in extraction: show reviewers which fields to check.
  • Hallucination hint: low-probability named entities or numbers flagged for verification.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Calibrate on labelled data (e.g. how often answers above 0.9 are correct), and consider sampling-based consistency (several samples agreeing) as another uncertainty signal (see Q39).

followUps.question: 🧪 A classifier's label logprobs are: "yes" −0.05, "no" −3.2. What's the implied probability of "yes", renormalised over the two?
followUps.html: e^−0.05 ≈ 0.951, e^−3.2 ≈ 0.041; renormalised, 0.951 / 0.992 ≈ 0.96. Useful as a score, but only trustworthy after checking calibration on labelled data.

followUps.question: "High logprob means the answer is right."
followUps.html: It means the model found the token likely given its training and the prompt. Models are often confidently wrong, especially on facts outside their knowledge. Calibrate before using as correctness.

followUps.question: How is perplexity related?
followUps.html: Perplexity is exp of the average negative logprob over a text: lower means the model found the text more predictable. Same numbers, used to measure a model on data rather than to judge one answer (see Q26).

followUps.question: How would you detect that the model is unsure without logprobs?
followUps.html: Sample several answers at moderate temperature and measure agreement (self-consistency), ask for a verbalised confidence (weak, but calibratable), or check against retrieved evidence. Each costs extra calls.

followUps.question: Would you build routing between a small and large model on logprobs?
followUps.html: Yes, if the small model exposes them and I've calibrated a threshold on a labelled set to hit a target escalation rate and accuracy. I'd monitor the escalation rate over time, because a model or prompt update shifts the distribution, and keep a fallback signal for providers that don't return logprobs.

dontSay: "Logprob is the probability the answer is correct."
Comparing joint probabilities of different-length answers.
A design that requires logprobs from every provider.

llm-foundations-q13.testing: what each stage teaches, and which problems belong at which stage.
llm-foundations-q13.trap: describing RLHF as where the model "learns facts."
llm-foundations-q13.spoken:
"Pretraining produces a base model: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens gives it knowledge and language ability, but it just continues text. Post-training turns that into an assistant, in stages that each teach something different.

First, supervised fine-tuning: tens of thousands to millions of curated prompt–response examples teach the format and behaviour — follow instructions, answer rather than continue, use the chat template, call tools.

Second, preference optimisation: humans or AI judges compare two responses, and the model is trained to prefer the better one. Classic RLHF trains a reward model on those comparisons and optimises the policy with PPO, with a KL penalty to stay near the SFT model. DPO and its variants optimise the preference objective directly without a separate reward model. This stage teaches which of several acceptable answers people prefer: helpfulness, tone, refusals.

Third, for reasoning models, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: the model is rewarded for correct answers on maths and code, which trains it to use long chains of thought.

Knowledge mostly comes from pretraining; post-training shapes how it's expressed. The recurring failures are reward hacking — the model optimises the judge's quirks, like length or flattery — and sycophancy.

As an application engineer, I mostly work at the prompt level, sometimes with SFT or LoRA for format and style, and rarely with preference tuning."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "Post-training teaches behaviour on top of pretrained knowledge: SFT for format, preference optimisation for which answer is preferred, RL on verifiable rewards for reasoning."

stages.name: The stages in order
stages.html:
Stage Data Teaches Typical scale
pretraining raw text, trillions of tokens knowledge, language, patterns months, thousands of GPUs
SFT curated prompt → response instruction following, format, tool use 10k–1M+ examples
preference (RLHF / DPO) pairs: chosen vs rejected preferred style, helpfulness, safety behaviour 100k+ comparisons
RL with verifiable rewards problems with checkable answers multi-step reasoning, long chains model-generated rollouts
safety / refusal tuning adversarial prompts + policy refusal boundaries mixed into the above

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
• Reward hacking: the policy exploits reward-model blind spots (longer answers, confident tone).
  • Sycophancy: agreeing with the user because raters preferred it.
  • Over-refusal: safety tuning that refuses harmless requests.
  • Alignment tax: some capability loss on benchmarks after heavy preference tuning.
  • Forgetting: narrow SFT degrading general skills (see Q17).

stages.name: What application teams actually touch
stages.claim: mostly prompts and small fine-tunes, rarely RL
stages.html:
Problem Right stage
wrong facts, missing domain knowledge not post-training: retrieval (Q24)
format, style, domain phrasing, a narrow task prompt first; then SFT/LoRA
preference between acceptable outputs at scale DPO on your pairs (rarely needed)
better reasoning on checkable tasks choose a reasoning model, not train one

💻 Prove it — an eval plan for an SFT decision (cells to measure):

Metric Prompt-only + SFT (LoRA)
task accuracy on held-out set measure measure
format validity measure measure
general-capability check (held-out general set) measure measure
cost per 1k requests measure measure

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Replacing human raters with AI feedback guided by written principles scales the preference stage (see Q32).

followUps.question: 🧪 A base model is given "What is the capital of France?" What might it output?
followUps.html: Often a continuation of a list of quiz questions — "What is the capital of Germany?" — because on the web that pattern continues that way. It knows Paris, but without SFT it doesn't behave as an answerer. That shows knowledge comes from pretraining and behaviour from post-training.

followUps.question: "RLHF is where the model learns facts."
followUps.html: Facts come overwhelmingly from pretraining. Preference optimisation changes which of the model's possible answers it prefers to give; it can make it more cautious or more assertive about facts, not add many new ones.

followUps.question: Why keep a KL penalty to the SFT model during RLHF?
followUps.html: Without it, the policy drifts toward whatever exploits the reward model, producing degenerate text. The KL term keeps outputs close to the fluent SFT distribution while still improving reward.

followUps.question: What changed with reasoning-model training?
followUps.html: RL on tasks with verifiable answers (maths, code tests) rewards reaching correct results, and models learn to produce long reasoning traces, backtrack and check work. It scales without human raters because the reward is automatic (see Q19).

followUps.question: Your team wants to "do RLHF" on customer feedback. What do you advise?
followUps.html: Start by finding what the feedback is about: facts (fix retrieval), format (prompt or SFT), or preferences between good answers. If it truly is preference, DPO on curated pairs with a held-out eval is far simpler than a reward model plus PPO. Budget most effort for data quality, and gate on general-capability evals to catch regressions.

dontSay: "SFT and RLHF are the same thing."
"We'll fine-tune it to know our documents."

links.label: RLHF and why it is unstable and expensive
links.target: 05-LLM-Production/04-Post-Training& Alignment/03-RLHF and why it is unstable and expensive

llm-foundations-q14.testing: mechanism-level difference, and that the choice is about stability, cost and data, not accuracy.
llm-foundations-q14.trap: framing it as "which gives a better model" — data quality dominates both.
llm-foundations-q14.spoken:
"Both learn from preference pairs — a prompt, a preferred answer and a rejected one. They differ in how.

RLHF trains a separate reward model to score answers, then optimises the language model with reinforcement learning, usually PPO, to maximise that reward while a KL penalty keeps it close to the starting model. That's four models in memory — policy, reference, reward and value — plus sampling in the loop. It's powerful, because it generates new answers online and can explore beyond the dataset, but it's unstable, expensive and full of hyperparameters, and it invites reward hacking.

DPO showed that the same objective can be optimised directly: a classification-style loss that increases the probability of the chosen answer relative to the rejected one, compared with a frozen reference model. No reward model, no RL loop, just supervised-style training on pairs. It's much simpler and cheaper, and it's what most teams use now.

The trade-off: DPO is offline — it learns only from the pairs you have — and can overfit to them. Online methods, including RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning, still matter where exploration helps. Variants like IPO, KTO and ORPO adjust for overfitting or unpaired data.

For an application team, I'd pick DPO, and spend the effort on the preference data, because that's what decides the outcome."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: online RL vs a direct offline loss
stages.html:
RLHF (PPO) DPO
reward model yes, trained separately no (implicit)
training loop sample → score → PPO update supervised loss on fixed pairs
models in memory policy, reference, reward, value policy, reference
stability sensitive, many hyperparameters stable, few hyperparameters (β)
data use online: new samples each step offline: the given pairs
failure mode reward hacking overfitting pairs, drifting on unseen prompts

stages.name: Where RLHF wins
stages.html:
• The policy generates fresh answers and gets feedback on them, so it can improve beyond the initial data distribution.
  • A reward model can be reused to score new data and rank samples (best-of-n).
  • Verifiable-reward RL (maths, code) is the online approach behind reasoning models.

stages.name: Where DPO wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the DPO loss on three cases (β = 0.1):

import math
def dpo_loss(pw, pl, rw, rl, beta=0.1):          # log-probs: policy/ref, chosen (w) / rejected (l)
    margin = beta * ((pw - rw) - (pl - rl))
    return -math.log(1 / (1 + math.exp(-margin)))
print(round(dpo_loss(-12.0, -15.0, -12.0, -15.0), 4))   # policy == reference
print(round(dpo_loss(-10.0, -18.0, -12.0, -15.0), 4))   # chosen up, rejected down
print(round(dpo_loss(-14.0, -13.0, -12.0, -15.0), 4))   # moved the wrong way
# → 0.6931
# → 0.4741
# → 0.913

Loss starts at ln 2, falls when the policy raises the chosen answer and lowers the rejected one relative to the reference, and rises when it does the opposite. That's the whole objective (Rafailov et al., 2023).

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: do you need exploration, or do you have good pairs?
stages.html:
• Good curated pairs, limited infra → DPO (or ORPO/KTO depending on data format).
  • Verifiable rewards and large compute → online RL.
  • Either way, the data decides: noisy or biased preferences (length, flattery) are learned faithfully.

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html: • Curate pairs from real outputs, dedupe, control for length bias; LoRA + DPO; evaluate on task, general capability and safety sets before rollout.

followUps.question: 🧪 In DPO, what happens to the loss if β is very large?
followUps.html: The margin is multiplied by β, so small log-ratio differences saturate the sigmoid quickly: the model is pushed hard to separate pairs and stays less anchored to the reference behaviour on those examples, raising overfitting risk. Small β keeps changes gentle. β is effectively the inverse strength of the KL constraint.

followUps.question: "DPO replaced RL, so RL is dead."
followUps.html: DPO replaced PPO-based RLHF for many preference-tuning jobs. RL is central to reasoning models (verifiable rewards) and still used by frontier labs for preference optimisation. The field uses both.

followUps.question: What is KTO for?
followUps.html: KTO learns from single examples labelled good or bad, not pairs. Useful when you have thumbs-up/down feedback rather than side-by-side comparisons.

followUps.question: How do you detect reward hacking or preference overfitting?
followUps.html: Watch output length and style drift, check held-out prompts with human or rubric review, and track general benchmarks. A rising reward score with flat human ratings is the signature.

followUps.question: Leadership asks for "our own RLHF". Budget it.
followUps.html: Most cost is data: thousands to tens of thousands of carefully labelled pairs, labeller guidelines, quality checks. Training with DPO + LoRA on an open model is modest. Add eval infrastructure and a rollout plan. Then compare against prompt changes and SFT, which often capture most of the gain for far less.
